title: Sequoia Capital Raises $7 Billion for AI-Focused Expansion Under New Leadership
excerpt: The Silicon Valley stalwart's first major fundraise under new co-stewards Alfred Lin and Pat Grady nearly doubles its previous expansion fund, as top VC firms collectively amass over $23 billion in four months.
body:
• Sequoia Capital has raised roughly $7 billion for a new expansion fund, nearly double its previous $3.4 billion vehicle from 2022, marking the first major fundraise under new co-stewards Alfred Lin and Pat Grady.
  • The fund will target late-stage investments in AI-focused companies across the U.S. and Europe, with existing bets on OpenAI and Anthropic — both reportedly eyeing 2026 public listings.
  • Sequoia's raise is part of a broader trend: Thrive Capital closed $10 billion in February and Founders Fund raised $6 billion in May, bringing the combined haul of three top VC firms to over $23 billion in four months.
  • Since 2020, Sequoia has distributed more than $43 billion back to its investors, positioning the firm as a net liquidity provider to its limited partners.

New Leaders, Bigger Bets

Sequoia Capital's new leadership is wasting no time putting its stamp on the 54-year-old firm. Alfred Lin and Pat Grady, who took over as co-stewards after Roelof Botha stepped down in November 2025, have raised roughly $7 billion for a new expansion fund — the largest of its kind in the firm's history and nearly double its previous comparable vehicle.

The fund will target what Sequoia calls its "expansion strategy" — late-stage investments in companies across the United States and Europe that have already reached significant scale. In the AI era, that means companies burning through capital at rates that would have been unimaginable a decade ago, and the firms backing them need to keep pace.

Where the Money Goes

A significant portion of the capital is expected to flow toward Sequoia's highest-profile AI bets. The firm was an early backer of both OpenAI and Anthropic, the two companies that have defined the generative AI race. Both are reportedly exploring public listings in 2026 — a development that could deliver enormous returns for the fund.

But Sequoia is not only swinging for the foundational AI heavyweights. The firm has also placed bets on Physical Intelligence, a Bay Area robotics startup, and Factory, which builds AI agents for enterprise engineering teams. The strategy reflects a conviction that the AI opportunity extends far beyond the model builders to the companies putting the technology to work.

"If they're excited, they're the most important people."

— Alfred Lin has emphasized that Sequoia focuses on DPI over AUM, with $43 billion distributed to investors since 2020

A Coordinated Read on the Market

Sequoia's fundraise does not exist in isolation. Thrive Capital, backed by Joshua Kushner, closed a $10 billion fund in February — its largest ever, nearly double its previous vehicle. In May, Peter Thiel's Founders Fund closed $6 billion, its largest haul in two decades, assembled in record time. Together, three of Silicon Valley's most selective venture firms raised over $23 billion in private capital in four months.

The coordinated scale of these raises is a signal. These are not generalist vehicles hedging across industries. They are concentrated bets on AI infrastructure, AI applications, defense technology, and the companies building the next computing paradigm. Founders Fund backed Anthropic at a reported $350 billion valuation and put $1 billion into defense firm Anduril. Thrive is investing across AI, space, robotics, and life sciences.

What It Means for India's Tech Ecosystem

Sequoia's evolution has direct implications for India's startup landscape. The firm split off its Indian and Southeast Asian operations into an independent entity, Peak XV Partners, in 2023 as part of a broader restructuring driven by geopolitical considerations. But the parent firm's AI-first thesis continues to influence where capital flows globally.

For Indian AI startups seeking late-stage funding, the message is mixed: there is more capital available than ever for AI companies that have achieved real scale, but Sequoia's expansion fund is focused on the U.S. and Europe. Indian founders building for global markets — particularly in AI infrastructure, enterprise software, and applied AI — may find themselves competing for a share of this capital pool, while those focused on domestic markets will increasingly look to Peak XV and other India-focused firms.

Lin, who ranks as the number one investor on the Midas List, has been vocal about his belief that AI represents the biggest paradigm shift of his career and that the next generation of great companies could be dramatically larger than today's giants. At Sequoia, the fund size now matches the ambition.
